docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page shows the electrical architecture of my subsystem for Team 102's Modular Spider Leg. In the team's hub-and-spoke layout, my board is the spoke on hub connector 3. It drives the leg's small linear actuator (the actuator) and measures leg motion with an accelerometer for jerk and impulse sensing (the sensor). Commands come from Preston's hub board over the ribbon cable.

The design follows the RAS 304 project requirements:

  • PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano as the microcontroller.
  • A 9 V barrel jack feeding a 5 V linear regulator, with a fuse and a power-status LED.
  • A 2x4 male IDC header using the class ribbon pinout.
  • No daughter boards: every peripheral, including the accelerometer, is placed directly on this PCB.

Parts were also chosen to stay within the team's $60–70 total budget.

The block diagram shows:

  • Power levels: my own 9 V adapter → barrel jack → fuse → L7805 linear regulator (5 V) for the motor driver, the actuator motor, and the Curiosity Nano. The Curiosity Nano's on-board regulator supplies 3.3 V to the accelerometer and the position potentiometer.
  • Actuator: an N20 gear motor with an M3 lead screw, driven by a TI DRV8833 H-bridge. A current-sense resistor allows stall detection.
  • Position feedback: a Bourns slide potentiometer whose slider moves with the actuator's lead-screw nut.
  • Sensor: an ST LIS3DH 3-axis accelerometer chip on SPI, with a data-ready interrupt.
  • Team connection: an 8-pin ribbon cable to Preston's hub board. It carries position commands in and jerk/impulse data out over UART.

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
• Closed-loop position control: the hub sends a target position over UART. The PIC compares it with the slide-pot reading on RA1, then drives the two PWM outputs (RC2, RD0) to move the lead screw forward or back.
  • Stall and fault protection (Req. 6.1): current through the DRV8833 flows through a 0.2 Ω sense resistor on AISEN. The PIC reads that voltage on RA0 and stops the motor if the current stays high, which indicates a stall. The same resistor also sets the driver's built-in current limit at about 1 A. The nFAULT pin (RB1) reports over-current or over-temperature, and the PIC then disables the driver through nSLEEP (RD1).
  • Jerk and impulse sensing: the LIS3DH data-ready interrupt (RB0) triggers an SPI read of acceleration at up to about 1.3 kHz. Jerk is found by differentiating acceleration, and impulse by integrating force (mass × acceleration) over the foot-contact time. The results are sent to the hub over UART.
  • Accelerometer soldering: the LIS3DHTR is a 3 × 3 mm LGA-16 package. Because daughter boards aren't allowed, it is soldered directly to the PCB with a stencil and hot air or reflow.
  • Speed vs. cost: an M3 lead screw moves 0.5 mm per turn, so a 300 RPM motor gives about 2.5 mm/s at full speed. That is slow, but adequate for a small demonstration leg, and much cheaper than a commercial linear actuator with built-in feedback (about $80 or more).

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
RAS 304 – Individual Datasheet (Kaushik) – Driver Nano 2: Linear Actuator A + Pressure Sensor Project: Single Robotic Spider Leg

Scope: this page covers only my individual board (Driver Nano 2). Team-level decisions live in the team repository. Prices were checked on 2026-10-19 and will change.

docs.title: 1. Subsystem summary
docs.text:
Driver Nano 2 receives a target position for Linear Actuator A from the Main Processor Nano over the team bus, drives the actuator with PWM and direction signals, reads the actuator's position feedback and a foot pressure sensor, decides whether contact or a force threshold has been reached, and reports status and pressure back to the Main Processor.

Project constraints that drive the selections:

  • Through-hole parts only (no daughter boards), PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano as the MCU.
  • External 9 V barrel-jack supply, on-board 5 V linear regulator, fuse and power indicator.
  • The Curiosity Nano runs its I/O and ADC at its target voltage, which is 3.3 V as shipped (Curiosity Nano user guide, section 3.3.1). Every analog signal into the MCU must stay at or below 3.3 V.
  • 2x4 IDC bus connector to the rest of the leg.

Assumptions to confirm with the team (they change the actuator and driver choices if they move):

  • Actuator A needs about 20 mm of stroke and no more than about 40 N at the foot.
  • The foot sensor is used for contact and threshold detection (per the software flow), not for calibrated force measurement.

docs.title: 2.1 [Actuator A subsystem] Linear actuator with position feedback
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Actuonix PQ12-P, 20 mm, 100:1, 6 V, potentiometer feedback$81.76 eachRobotShop product page · PQ12 datasheet • Rated 6 V, which matches what the motor sees from a 9 V rail after the bipolar driver's saturation drop (see choice rationale)• Built-in 5 kΩ position potentiometer gives closed-loop feedback with one ADC pin and no extra sensor• Peak power point of 40 N at 6 mm/s, 10 mm/s no load, enough for a leg joint assumption of about 40 N• Stall current of only 550 mA at 6 V keeps the supply and driver small• Compact 20 mm stroke body, easy to mount on a printed leg • 20% maximum duty cycle in the datasheet, so firmware must limit continuous driving• Potentiometer is 5 kΩ ±50%, so each unit needs calibration• Datasheet gives no input voltage tolerance, so firmware must cap PWM duty• Expensive for a student project• Only 20 mm of stroke limits leg range Option 2. Actuonix PQ12-P, 20 mm, 100:1, 12 V, potentiometer feedback$81.76 eachRobotShop product page · PQ12 datasheet • Same body, feedback pot and mounting as Option 1• Low stall current of 210 mA at 12 V, easy on the supply• Peak power point of 40 N at 6 mm/s at its rated 12 V • Needs 12 V, but the project supply is 9 V and the driver drops about 2.5 to 3.5 V, so the motor would see only about 6 V, half its rating, and lose speed and force• Adding a boost converter would break the single 9 V and 5 V rail plan• Same 20% duty cycle and pot tolerance limits as Option 1• Same price as the 6 V version with no benefit at 9 V Option 3. Actuonix L12-P, 50 mm, 100:1, 12 V, analog position feedback$100.63 eachRobotShop product page (datasheet linked from the listing) • 50 mm of stroke gives more leg travel• Fast: 23 mm/s no load• Low 200 mA stall current at 12 V• Analog position output suits the ADC • 12 V rating has the same under-voltage problem as Option 2• Peak power point is only 23 N at 6 mm/s, lower than the PQ12• Largest and most expensive option, harder to fit on a spider leg• Longer body adds mass at the joint Option 4 (custom). DC gearmotor + lead screw + linear potentiometer, built in-houseNot a commercial part, no single product link or unit price • Fully tunable stroke, speed and force• Could run directly at 6 V to 9 V• Parts are individually replaceable • Needs a custom mechanical design (screw, nut, guides, coupling), which is a large schedule risk this semester• Needs its own position sensing and end stops• Backlash and alignment problems likely• Total cost and size are unknown until designed

Choice: Option 1, Actuonix PQ12-P 6 V, 100:1 [Actuator A subsystem]

Rationale: The bipolar H-bridge I chose (section 2.2) drops roughly 2.6 to 3.6 V in total near 0.6 A (high-side 1.4 to 1.8 V plus low-side 1.2 to 1.8 V, datasheet ranges for this driver family), so a 9 V rail delivers about 5.4 to 6.4 V to the motor. That matches the 6 V rating, so the actuator reaches its rated 40 N and 10 mm/s peak-power point. The 12 V versions would run at about half their rated voltage. The built-in potentiometer lets Driver Nano 2 report position back to the Main Processor with a single ADC pin. I accept the 20% duty cycle and the pot tolerance as limits, and handle them with firmware duty-cycle limiting and a per-unit calibration. The 6 V actuator on the 9 V rail needs a bench check of the motor-terminal voltage before full-speed testing.

docs.title: 2.2 [Actuator A subsystem] Motor driver (H-bridge)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. TI SN754410NE quadruple half-H driver, DIP-16$4.50 eachSparkFun product page · TI datasheet • 1 A continuous per channel (2 A peak), about 1.7 times the 550 to 600 mA actuator stall current• Built-in clamp diodes, so no external flyback diodes• Logic high threshold of 2 V minimum works with the Nano's 3.3 V outputs• 4.5 to 36 V motor supply covers the 9 V rail• Thermal shutdown built in• Through-hole DIP-16, pin-compatible with the L293D as a fallback • Bipolar outputs drop about 2.6 to 3.6 V total, so efficiency is poor and the driver dissipates roughly 1.5 to 2 W at stall• Needs the four ground pins soldered to a copper pour for heat sinking• Quiescent supply current is high for a logic IC (tens of mA)• No built-in current sensing Option 2. L293D dual H-bridge, DIP-16$8.95 each (price as listed)Adafruit product page · TI datasheet • Internal kickback diodes• 4.5 to 36 V motor supply• Well documented, many examples• Same DIP-16 footprint as Option 1 • Only 600 mA continuous per channel, which is no margin against a 550 to 600 mA stall• 1.2 A peak limit is only for 100 µs• Logic high threshold of 2.3 V is closer to the 3.3 V output level• More expensive than the SN754410 on this listing Option 3. ST L298N dual full bridge, Multiwatt-15$14.42 eachNewark product page · ST product page and datasheet • 2 A continuous per channel, large margin• Sense pins allow a shunt resistor for current monitoring• Handles up to 46 V • Needs four external fast diodes for the inductive load• Total saturation drop up to 3.2 V at 1 A, which is large for a 9 V rail• High quiescent current on both supplies (tens of mA)• Bulky vertical Multiwatt package and the most expensive option• Overkill for a 550 mA actuator Option 4 (custom). Discrete MOSFET H-bridge (logic-level N-FETs and P-FETs with gate drive)Not a single commercial part, no unit price • Very low voltage drop, so the motor sees nearly the full 9 V and less heat is dissipated• Scales to higher current later • Needs shoot-through protection and level-shifted gate drive for the high side• Many more parts and board area• Higher design and debug risk on a first board• With almost no drop, a 6 V motor would see nearly the full 9 V, so the PWM duty would have to be capped tightly to avoid overvoltage

Choice: Option 1, SN754410NE [Actuator A subsystem]

Rationale: It is the only through-hole driver here that gives real current margin (1 A continuous against about 0.6 A stall) without external diodes or heavy packaging. Its saturation drop is the reason the 6 V actuator works from a 9 V rail. The 2 V logic threshold is compatible with the Nano's 3.3 V I/O, and it is pin-compatible with the L293D if I need a different supplier. The drawbacks (power dissipation and quiescent current) are handled by a copper pour on the ground pins, firmware duty-cycle limits, and the budget in the Power Budget page.

docs.title: 2.3 [Pressure sensor subsystem] Pressure / force sensor
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Interlink FSR 402 force-sensing resistor$13.49 eachPololu product page · Interlink manufacturer page • Responds from about 0.2 N to 20 N, which suits foot contact detection• 0.58 in diameter active area is large enough to catch a foot strike• Thin and flexible, easy to mount on the foot• Simple resistive output, so a divider and one op-amp stage is enough• Lower total cost than the load cell once the load cell's instrumentation amplifier is counted, and about 40% less than the FlexiForce • Resistance falls from over 1 MΩ unloaded to hundreds of ohms under heavy pressure, so the front end must handle a wide range• Limited absolute accuracy and drift, so it suits thresholds better than calibrated force• Fragile tail and connector area, needs strain relief Option 2. Tekscan FlexiForce A201-100 (100 lb)$22.95 eachSparkFun product page · Datasheet • Better repeatability than a typical FSR for the same circuit• 0 to 100 lb range survives heavy foot loads• Published datasheet with a recommended op-amp circuit • 100 lb range is far above the expected foot load, so light contact gives a small signal• About 70% more expensive than the FSR 402• Small sensing area at the tip can miss off-center contact• Still needs op-amp conditioning Option 3. SparkFun TAL220 10 kg bar load cell$12.95 eachSparkFun product page · Datasheet • Most accurate and linear of the three, suitable for real force measurement• 10 kg capacity with strain-gauge bridge, so stable over time• Inexpensive for a bridge sensor of this accuracy • Millivolt-level bridge output needs a custom instrumentation amplifier with several op-amps or a dedicated IC, which adds board area and risk• 80 mm bar needs a proper mechanical mount and load path, awkward on a small leg foot• Heavy compared with a film sensor• Overscoped for contact detection

Choice: Option 1, Interlink FSR 402 [Pressure sensor subsystem]

Rationale: The software flow only asks whether contact is detected or a threshold is reached, so absolute accuracy matters less than sensitivity at low force and a simple front end. The FSR 402's 0.2 N to 20 N range matches a foot contact event, it is flat and light enough for a leg, and it has the lowest total cost once the load cell's extra amplifier circuitry is counted. The load cell would be more accurate but needs a custom instrumentation amplifier and a mount the leg does not have room for. The FlexiForce's 100 lb range is too coarse for light contact. I accept the FSR's drift and nonlinearity because the firmware compares against a threshold and can recalibrate the baseline at startup.

docs.title: 2.4 [Pressure sensor subsystem] Signal-conditioning op-amp
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Microchip MCP6002-I/P dual op-amp, DIP-8$0.41 eachTME product page · Datasheet • Runs from 1.8 to 6 V, so it can sit on the Nano's 3.3 V rail and its output can never exceed what the ADC allows• Rail-to-rail input and output• 1 MHz bandwidth, plenty for a force signal• Dual package gives a spare amplifier for a second filter stage• Very low supply current• Very inexpensive • Only 1 MHz, not suited to later high-speed ideas• Low output drive, fine for an ADC but not for loads• Limited to 6 V maximum supply Option 2. TI LM358P dual op-amp, DIP-8$0.28 eachTME product page · Datasheet • Lowest price and widely available• Input range includes ground, convenient for single-supply sensing• 3 to 32 V supply range is flexible • Output cannot swing within about 1.5 V of its positive supply, so on 3.3 V it only reaches about 1.8 V, which wastes ADC range• On the 5 V rail the output can reach about 3.5 V, above the Nano's 3.3 V limit, so it would need a clamp• Only 0.7 MHz bandwidth for the legacy part• Higher quiescent current than the MCP6002 Option 3. Microchip MCP6022-I/P dual op-amp, DIP-8$1.70 eachTME product page · Datasheet (MCP6021/2/3/4 family) • 2.5 to 5.5 V supply, rail-to-rail, works on 3.3 V• 10 MHz bandwidth leaves room for faster filtering• Lower noise for small signals • About four times the price of the MCP6002• Draws more supply current• Bandwidth is more than a force signal needs

Choice: Option 1, MCP6002-I/P [Pressure sensor subsystem]

Rationale: The key constraint is that the Nano's ADC only accepts up to 3.3 V. The MCP6002 runs directly from the 3.3 V rail with rail-to-rail output, so its output physically cannot exceed the ADC range, and no clamp is needed. The LM358P cannot give a useful swing at 3.3 V, and on 5 V it could overdrive the input. The MCP6022's extra bandwidth does not help a slowly varying force signal. The spare amplifier in the package is available for a second filter stage if the FSR signal is noisy.

docs.title: 2.5 [Power subsystem] 5 V linear voltage regulator
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. ST L7805CV 5 V regulator, TO-220$0.65 eachJameco product page · ST datasheet • Up to 1.5 A with internal current limiting and thermal shutdown• Specified for 7 to 18 V input, which brackets the 9 V adapter• Output capacitor only needed for transient response, so it is forgiving• Very inexpensive and easy to source• TO-220 takes a heatsink if needed • Dropout of about 2 V at 1 A, so it needs more than 7 V in• Quiescent current of about 8 mA• Dissipates (9 V − 5 V) × load, which is about 0.9 W at my worst case• Thermal resistance of about 50 °C/W without a heatsink Option 2. TI LM2940CT-5.0 low-dropout 5 V regulator, TO-220$1.94 eachDigi-Key product page · TI datasheet • Dropout of about 1 V at 1 A, so it still regulates if the supply sags• 1 A output, up to 26 V input• Same TO-220 footprint as Option 1 • Higher quiescent current (about 15 mA)• More than twice the price of the L7805CV• Low-dropout designs are more sensitive to output capacitor choice, so the datasheet capacitor requirement must be followed• Dropout advantage is unused with a regulated 9 V supply

Choice: Option 1, L7805CV [Power subsystem]

Rationale: The input is a regulated 9 V adapter, so there is 4 V of headroom over the L7805's 2 V dropout and low dropout buys nothing. My worst-case 5 V load with margin is about 0.22 A, giving about 0.87 W dissipated and a junction rise of about 43 °C at 50 °C/W, which is acceptable without a heatsink (see the Power Budget). It is the least expensive option, forgiving on capacitors, and has built-in current limiting and thermal shutdown.

docs.title: 2.6 [Power subsystem] External 9 V power source
docs.text:
USB power packs are not allowed for this project, so all options are wall adapters.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Adafruit 9 V 1 A regulated adapter, 5.5 × 2.1 mm, center-positive$8.95 eachAdafruit product page • Regulated output• Barrel size and positive tip are stated on the page• UL listed• Lowest price • 1 A is not enough: my worst-case need with margin is about 1.02 A, so remaining current would be negative• No headroom for added sensors later Option 2. Pololu 9 V 1 A regulated adapter, 5.5 × 2.1 mm, center-positive$11.11 eachPololu product page • Regulated, polarity stated, 1.5 m cord• Light, small body• Reliable supplier • Same 1 A limit fails the budget• Most expensive of the three Option 3. SparkFun 9 V 2 A regulated adapter, 5.5 × 2.1 mm$10.95 eachSparkFun product page · Datasheet • 2 A leaves about 980 mA of margin after my 25% safety factor• Regulated output• Room for stall-current surges and later changes • Plug polarity is not stated on the product page, so it must be checked before connecting• Larger body than the 1 A adapters

Choice: Option 3, SparkFun 9 V 2 A adapter [Power subsystem]

Rationale: The budget (see Power Budget) needs about 1.02 A from the supply including the 25% margin, which fails both 1 A adapters and passes the 2 A unit with about 0.98 A to spare. Before using it, I will check the polarity in its datasheet and with a multimeter, since the barrel jack and reverse-polarity protection assume center-positive.

Estimates marked "est." should be replaced with measured values once the board is built. These numbers still need to be copied into the course's power budget spreadsheet template.

docs.title: Power architecture
docs.text:
• One external source: a 9 V wall adapter on the barrel jack (the course supply).
  • Two rails: 9 V (raw adapter voltage) and 5 V (L7805CV linear regulator from the 9 V rail).
  • The Curiosity Nano takes the 5 V rail on its VBUS pin and makes its own 3.3 V (VTG), which powers the MCP6002 and the actuator potentiometer reference, so all analog signals stay within the ADC range. That 3.3 V load is counted on the 5 V rail below because the Nano's regulator draws it from the 5 V input.

Rail Choice Rationale 5 V ST L7805CV (TO-220) Specified for 7 to 18 V input, so the 9 V adapter has 4 V of headroom over its 2 V dropout. Rated up to 1.5 A against a 0.22 A load with margin. Has internal current limiting and thermal shutdown. Compared with the LM2940CT-5.0 in the Component Selection page. 9 V Straight from the wall adapter The actuator and driver run directly from the adapter, so no second regulator is needed

Regulator check:

Quantity Value Load current including margin 216.9 mA Regulator quiescent current (datasheet, about 8 mA) × 1.25 10 mA Power dissipated: (9 V − 5 V) × 0.217 A 0.87 W Junction rise at 50 °C/W (TO-220, no heatsink) about 43 °C Junction temperature at 40 °C ambient about 83 °C (limit 125 °C)

docs.title: Section D. External power source
docs.text:
Item Value Source choice SparkFun 9 V 2 A regulated wall adapter Current into 9 V rail loads (with margin) 791.3 mA Current into the L7805CV input: (173.5 + 8) × 1.25 226.9 mA Total required from adapter 1018.1 mA Adapter capacity 2000 mA Total remaining current available 981.9 mA (not negative)

For comparison, a 1 A adapter would leave 1000 − 1018.1 = −18.1 mA, which fails the check. That is why the 2 A adapter was selected. The adapter's plug polarity must be confirmed before first power-up (see the Component Selection page).

docs.title: Section E. Battery life
docs.text: Not applicable. The design runs from a wall adapter and has no battery.

  3. Measure the motor-terminal voltage and stall current of the 6 V actuator on the 9 V rail, and cap the PWM duty accordingly.
  4. Copy these numbers into the course power budget spreadsheet template.
